# Executive Summary

## Overview Summary

This project analyzed drinking water violation data from the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS). 
The target audience of this project is people who have a vested interest in understanding patterns in drinking water contamination violations including environmental researchers, public health officials, regulatory agencies, and policymakers. 
In order to discern these patterns, raw data from SDWIS had to be cleaned, merged, and transformed. 
These processes allowed for identification of trends in contaminant violations, facility characteristics, and water source types through exploratory data analysis (EDA).

The analysis used SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv, SDWA_FACILITIES.csv, and SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv which were pulled directly from the EPA SDWIS. 
The violations dataset contained information about contaminant violations, including public water system identifiers, facility identifiers, contaminant codes, violation dates, contaminant measurements, and measurement units. 
The facilities dataset contained information describing water system facilities, including facility names, operational status, facility types, and water source types. 
The geographic dataset provided county-level geographic information for public water systems. These datasets were filtered, cleaned, and merged into one dataset using shared identifiers like PWSID and FACILITY_ID.

Before performing any data analysis, the imported data needed to be cleaned and transformed. 
Records with incorrectly formatted PWSID values were removed. 
Duplicates and extreme invalid outlier measurements were removed. 
Columns were reordered and renamed for readability and clarity. 
Exploratory data analysis was then conducted using descriptive statistics and visualizations including histograms, barplots, boxplots, and cross-tabulations.

Post-transformation, exploratory data analysis was used to identify patterns in the data. 
Contaminant measures were right skewed where it was observed that most records indicated a low contaminant concentration value and there were relatively few records indicating high contaminant concentration value. 
Active facilities largely outnumber inactive facilities meeting expectations that active systems will continue reporting violations. 
Groundwater systems (GW) accounted for most of the known water source records and exhibited the highest average contaminant measurements among water types. 
The most common contaminants included TTHM, Arsenic, Total Haloacetic Acids (HAA5), and Nitrate. This communicated that the majority of water quality violations recorded were from a small subset of contaminants. 

Preparing the data for analysis proved to be a massive challenge for the project. 
Transforming the data required resolving issues with duplicates, missing values, invalid measurements, and datatypes. 
Examining the relationships between contaminant levels, facility types, and water source categories was interesting as these trends and relationships can be used to support public health research, water system management, and future environmental decision making.

## Well-Formulated Audience and Purpose

### Target Audience

The primary audience for this project includes:
- Environmental researchers 
- Public health officials 
- Regulatory agencies
- Policaymakers and lawmakers 

These groups may use the analysis to better understand drinking water contamination trends, reporting patterns, and infrastructure risks associated with public water systems

### Purpose

The purpose of the project was to:
1. collect and integrate EPA drinking water violation datasets 
2. clean and transform the data into a usable dataset 
3. perform exploratory data analysis on contaminant violations and facility characteristics
4. identify patterns, trends, and irregularities related to contaminant measurements, water sources, and facility operations
The project focused on using EDA techniques to better understand the structure, quality, and environmental significance of the drinking water violation data.

## Achieved Purpose

The project successfully achieved its intended purpose by producing a cleaned and merged analytical dataset and conducting comprehensive exploratory data analysis on the final variables. 
This project was also able to navigate challenges including missing data, invalid values, outlier values, duplicate records, and datatype inconsistencies. 
The analysis identified meaningful trends in contaminant measurements, facility activity, water source distributions, and commonly occurring contaminants. 
Multiple statistical summaries and visualizations were used to examine both individual variable distributions and relationships between variables, including comparisons of contaminant measurements across water source types and facility categories.

# Source(s) & Extraction

## Data Source
The data sources can be downloaded as a .zip from https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads#downloads
under the "Drinking Water Data Downloads" section.

## Data Generation and Collection

The data was generated when contaminants entered drinking water. The data is collected by any entity required by the
Safe Water Drinking Act to enforce drinking water regulations. Each entity reports their data to the EPA, which is
then stored in the SDWIS Fed Data Warehouse.

Source: https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/safe-drinking-water-information-system-sdwis-federal-reporting

## Original Variables

### SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv
- PWSID: Unique code for a public water system. Consists of a two-letter state or region code and 7 digits.
- VIOLATION_ID: Identifier for a violation. Series of digits, variable length.
- FACILITY_ID: Identifier for a facility in a public water system. Series of digits, variable length.
- NON_COMPL_PER_BEGIN_DATE: Date when violation has been identified. 2 digit month/2 digit day/4 digit year.
- NON_COMPL_PER_END_DATE: Date when violation has ended. Ongoing violations have a null value. 2 digit month/2 digit day/4 digit year.
- CONTAMINANT_CODE: Code representing a contaminant. Series of digits, variable length.
- VIOL_MEASURE: The amount of the contaminant. Decimal.
- UNIT_OF_MEASURE: The unit of measure. String.

### SDWA_FACILITIES.csv
- PWSID: Unique code for a public water system. Consists of a two-letter state or region code and 7 digits.
- FACILITY_ID: Identifier for a facility in a public water system. Series of digits, variable length.
- FACILITY_NAME: The name of the facility. String. 
- FACILITY_ACTIVITY_CODE: A single-letter code identifying the facility's operating status.
- FACILITY_TYPE_CODE: A two-letter code identifying the type of facility.
- WATER_TYPE_CODE: A two-letter code identifying the water source.

### SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv
- PWSID: Unique code for a public water system. Consists of a two-letter state or region code and 7 digits.
- COUNTY_SERVED: The county served by the public water system.

## Shrinking Data
The original data is large and must be shrunk down. **Do not run this code**. It has already been run and the datasets it created have been provided in the repository.
The code is here to demonstrate how the data was shrunk.

Each dataset was loaded using read_csv(). The columns of interest were selected with the usecols parameter. The datatype of the FACILITY_ID column in the violations dataframe
was cast as a string. This will be important later. The violations dataframe's null values and duplicate rows were dropped to shrink the dataframe further.

The PWSID and FACILITY_ID columns uniquely identify public water system facilities. To shrink the facilities and locations dataframes, a list of unique PWSID and FACILITY_ID values were created
from the violations dataframe. The PWSID and FACILITY_ID columns in the facilities and locations dataframes are strings, so the unique values must also be strings. The dataframes were filtered by selected rows 
where their values are present in the unique values list.

The dataframes were exported as csv files.

```{python}
violations = pd.read_csv('SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv',
                         usecols=['PWSID', 'VIOLATION_ID', 'FACILITY_ID', 'NON_COMPL_PER_BEGIN_DATE', 'NON_COMPL_PER_END_DATE',
                                  'CONTAMINANT_CODE', 'VIOL_MEASURE', 'UNIT_OF_MEASURE'],
                         dtype={'FACILITY_ID': 'str'}).dropna().drop_duplicates()


# get unique PWSID and FACILITY_ID
sys_id = violations['PWSID'].unique().tolist()
fac_id = violations['FACILITY_ID'].unique().tolist()


facilities = pd.read_csv('SDWA_FACILITIES.csv',
                         usecols=['PWSID', 'FACILITY_ID', 'FACILITY_NAME',
                                  'FACILITY_ACTIVITY_CODE', 'FACILITY_TYPE_CODE',
                                  'WATER_TYPE_CODE'])
# select rows where PWSID and FACILITY_ID are in violations
facilities = facilities[facilities['PWSID'].isin(sys_id) & facilities['FACILITY_ID'].isin(fac_id)]


locations = pd.read_csv('SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv',
                        usecols=['PWSID', 'COUNTY_SERVED'])
# select rows where PWSID are in violations
locations = locations[locations['PWSID'].isin(sys_id)]


facilities.to_csv('facilities.csv', index=False)
locations.to_csv('locations.csv', index=False)
violations.to_csv('violations.csv', index=False)
```

## Extracting & Merging
Each CSV was loaded using read_csv(). The datatype of each dataframe's columns were printed to identify columns with incorrect datatypes. Next, the unique values of columns that
can be represented categorically were printed to verify that they had a fixed set of values. Datatypes were then changed.

The CONTAMINANT_CODE column in the violations dataframe required additional transformations. This column was formatted as a decimal, but the same column in the contaminant_codes
dataframe was formatted as a string. To resolve this discrepancy, the violation dataframe's column was cast as a string and the decimal point and following values were replaced with a blank string
by a regular expression. This method was necessary because some values begin with "0" and converting the column to an integer would remove the "0", therefore altering the contaminant code.

Before merging the dataframes, the contaminant_codes dataframe was filtered. This dataframe contains other reference codes, which were filtered out by selecting rows
where the VALUE_TYPE column was equal to "CONTAMINANT_CODE". The VALUE_CODE and VALUE_DESCRIPTION columns were then selected.

The dataframes were then merged. The facilities and locations dataframes were inner merged on the PWSID column. The resulting dataframe, merged_df, was inner merged with the violations dataframe
on the PWSID and FACILITY_ID columns. Lastly, merged_df was left merged with the contaminant_codes dataframe; the left dataframe (merged_df) merged on the "CONTAMINANT_CODE" column and the right dataframe (contaminant_codes) merged on the "VALUE_CODE" column.


```{python}
import pandas as pd

facilities = pd.read_csv('data/facilities.csv')
locations = pd.read_csv('data/locations.csv')
# set dtype to resolve mixed type warning
violations = pd.read_csv('data/violations.csv', dtype={'VIOLATION_ID': 'str'})
# set dtype to resolve mixed type warning
contaminant_codes = pd.read_csv('data/SDWA_REF_CODE_VALUES.csv', dtype={'VALUE_CODE': 'str'})

# output each dataframe's data types 
print(f'facilities:\n{facilities.dtypes}\n\nlocations:\n{locations.dtypes}\n\nviolations:\n{violations.dtypes}\n\ncodes:\n{contaminant_codes.dtypes}\n')

# view unique values to determine whether category is proper dtype- need small set of fixed values
print(f'FACILITY_ACTIVITY_CODE: {facilities['FACILITY_ACTIVITY_CODE'].unique()}')
print(f'FACILITY_TYPE_CODE: {facilities['FACILITY_TYPE_CODE'].unique()}')
print(f'WATER_TYPE_CODE: {facilities['WATER_TYPE_CODE'].unique()}')
print(f'CONTAMINANT_CODE: {violations['CONTAMINANT_CODE'].unique()}')
print(f'UNIT_OF_MEASURE: {violations['UNIT_OF_MEASURE'].unique()}')
print('\n')

# change dtypes
facilities = facilities.astype(dtype={'FACILITY_ID': 'str',
                                'FACILITY_ACTIVITY_CODE': 'category',
                                'FACILITY_TYPE_CODE': 'category',
                                'WATER_TYPE_CODE': 'category'})

violations = violations.astype(dtype={'FACILITY_ID': 'str',                   
                                'NON_COMPL_PER_BEGIN_DATE': 'datetime64[ms]',
                                'NON_COMPL_PER_END_DATE': 'datetime64[ms]',
                                'CONTAMINANT_CODE': 'str',
                                'UNIT_OF_MEASURE': 'category'})
# remove decimal from CONTAMINANT_CODE                              
violations['CONTAMINANT_CODE'] = violations['CONTAMINANT_CODE'].str.replace('\.\d+', '', regex=True)                               

# get only contaminant codes
contaminant_codes = contaminant_codes[contaminant_codes['VALUE_TYPE'] == 'CONTAMINANT_CODE'][['VALUE_CODE', 'VALUE_DESCRIPTION']]

# merge dataframes
merged_df = pd.merge(facilities, locations, on='PWSID')
merged_df = pd.merge(merged_df, violations, on=['PWSID', 'FACILITY_ID'])
merged_df = pd.merge(merged_df, contaminant_codes, how='left', left_on='CONTAMINANT_CODE', right_on='VALUE_CODE')
print(merged_df)
```

# Transformation Processes

PWSID is formatted as 2 letters followed by 7 digits. Rows that didn't follow this format were removed by a regular expression that matched
2 A-Z characters followed by 7 digits from the beginning of the string.

Outliers in the VIOL_MEASURE column were found by finding its minimum and maximum values. The maximum value was 99,999, so the values were investigated further by printing values
larger than 1000. The resulting set returned a variety of measurements, but 99,999 was a repeated value that had a null VALUE_CODE and VALUE_DESCRIPTION. Rows with this value were removed
because they are likely incorrect.

The VALUE_CODE column, which originated from the contaminant_codes dataframe, was removed because it is a duplicate of the CONTAMINANT_CODE column.

The columns were reordered and renamed. They were reordered to place similar columns together, such as FACILITY_ID and FACILITY_NAME. The column names were converted to lowercase and
some were shortened or simplified to make the column's purpose clearer. facility_activity_code in this data is equal to either A (active) or I (inactive), so it was changed to "facility_status".
non_compl_per_begin_date and non_compl_per_end_date were shortened to "begin_date" and "end_date" respectively. value_description was changed to "contaminant_name" because the values in this
column are names, not descriptions. viol_measure was changed to "measure". unit_of_measure was changed to "unit" because its values and position next to the measurement column allow its meaning to be assumed.

```{python}
# PWSID must be 2 letter state/region code and 7 digits
merged_df = merged_df[merged_df['PWSID'].str.match('[A-Z]{2}\d{7}')]

# find outliers
print(merged_df['VIOL_MEASURE'].describe())
print(merged_df[merged_df['VIOL_MEASURE'] > 1000])
# remove outliers
merged_df = merged_df[merged_df['VIOL_MEASURE'] < 99999]

# remove VALUE_CODE column- redundant
merged_df = merged_df.drop(['VALUE_CODE'], axis=1)

# reorder columns
merged_df = merged_df[['PWSID', 'VIOLATION_ID', 'FACILITY_ID', 'FACILITY_NAME', 'COUNTY_SERVED', 'FACILITY_ACTIVITY_CODE',
              'FACILITY_TYPE_CODE', 'WATER_TYPE_CODE', 'NON_COMPL_PER_BEGIN_DATE', 'NON_COMPL_PER_END_DATE',
              'CONTAMINANT_CODE', 'VALUE_DESCRIPTION', 'VIOL_MEASURE', 'UNIT_OF_MEASURE']]

# rename columns
merged_df.columns = merged_df.columns.str.lower()  
merged_df = merged_df.rename(columns={'facility_activity_code': 'facility_status',
                              'non_compl_per_begin_date': 'begin_date',
                              'non_compl_per_end_date': 'end_date',
                              'value_description': 'contaminant_name',
                              'viol_measure': 'measure',
                              'unit_of_measure': 'unit'})
                            
print(merged_df)                              
```

# Analysis & Evaluation

### Variables: 
- measure (float): the amount of the contaminant detected
- pwsid (str): identifier for a public water system
- facility_id (str): identifier for a facility within a public water system
- facility_name (str): name of the facility associated with the violation
- facility_status (str): indicates activeness of facility (A = Active, I = Inactive)
- facility_type_code (str): type of facility (DS = Distribution System, TP = Treatment Plant, WL = Well, SS = Sampling Station)
- water_type_code (str): source or type of water (GW = Ground Water, SW = Surface Water, GU = Groundwater Under Influence)
- contaminant_code (str): code for contaminant
- contaminant_name (str): name of contaminant


## Descriptive EDA statistics

The Descriptive EDA statistics section summarized key variables from the dataset.
Computed min, max, mean, median, and missing values on 'measure' variable that identified the detected amount of contaminant.
Generated frequency tables for categorical variables. 
Calculated average contaminant measurement grouped by water type .
Created a cross-tabulation to show the distribution of facility status across different water types.

```{python}

#import pandas
import pandas as pd

# load final dataset
df = merged_df.copy()

# create a list of all of the numeric variables in the dataset
numeric_cols = ['measure']

# print summary statistics for each measure
for col in numeric_cols:
    print(f'\nSummary statistics for {col}')
    print(f'Minimum: {df[col].min()}')
    print(f'Maximum: {df[col].max()}')
    print(f'Mean: {df[col].mean()}')
    print(f'Median: {df[col].median()}')
    print(f'Missing values: {df[col].isna().sum()}')

# create a list of all categorical variables in dataset
categorical_cols = [
    'pwsid',
    'facility_id',
    'facility_name',
    'county_served',
    'facility_status',
    'facility_type_code',
    'water_type_code',
    'contaminant_code',
    'contaminant_name',
]

# print frequecies for categorical values
for col in categorical_cols:
    print(f'\nFrequency table for {col}')
    print(df[col].value_counts(dropna=False).sort_values(ascending=False))

# create a list for columns thatshave date values
date_cols = ['begin_date', 'end_date']

# print earliest recorded date, latest recorded date and number of missing dates
for col in date_cols:
    print(f'\nSummary statistics for {col}')
    print(f'Earliest date: {df[col].min()}')
    print(f'Latest date: {df[col].max()}')
    print(f'Missing values: {df[col].isna().sum()}')

# group data by water_type_code and calculate the average contaminant measurement (measure) for each water type

# average contaminant measure by water type
avg_measure = df.groupby('water_type_code')['measure'].mean()
print('\nAverage measure by water type')
print(avg_measure)

# cross-tabulation between facility status and water type
cross_tab = pd.crosstab(df['facility_status'], df['water_type_code'])
print('\nCross-tabulation')
print(cross_tab)

```

## Descriptive EDA narrative

The descriptive exploratory data analysis demonstrated important patterns in the drinking water violations dataset. 

### Numerical Variables
A log-transformed histogram was used to make the data easier to visualize because it reduced the effect of the extremely large values and made the smaller measurement patterns easier to see.
The variable measure, representing contaminant measurement levels, showed a right skewed distribution. This right-hand skewedness was expected because there was a higher likelihood of there being more reporting of small amounts of contaminants than reporting of large amounts of contaminants. 
The middle value (median) of the measurements was only 0.156, but the largest value was 16,698, indicating the possibility of outliers. 

### Categorical Variables
The categorical variables related to facility information also demonstrated important patterns. 
For the facility_status variable, the number of active facilities largely outnumbered the number of inactive facilities. 
This distribution result was expected because it is more likely that active facilities will continue to monitor and report violations whereas inactive facilities may not have the means or need to monitor or report water quality measures. 

The facility_type_code visualization showed that most of the violations reported came from a small subgroup of facility types. 
These facility types include distribution systems (DS), sampling stations (SS), treatment plants (TP), and wells (WL). 
This pattern is plausible because these specific facility types are responsible for drinking water infrastructure. 
This responsibility means that these facilities may be required to be more stringent about their water quality reporting and monitoring. 

The water_type_code variable showed an unexpected pattern because most records were missing a water type value (NaN). 
Of the records that did include a water type, almost all were labeled as groundwater (GW), while very few were surface water (SW) or purchased groundwater (GU). 
This could mean that many water systems did not report their water source type, or that the dataset mainly contains groundwater systems. 
The relationship analysis further showed that groundwater systems had the highest average contaminant measurements, with an average value of approximately 21.16, compared to 6.54 for surface water systems. 
The boxplot showed that groundwater systems also had the widest range of measurement values and the largest extreme contaminant measurements possibly indicating outliers. 

The contaminant variables (contaminant_code and contaminant_name) were used to plot the top 10 contaminants measured in the dataset. 
TTHM, Arsenic, Total Haloacetic Acids (HAA5), and Nitrate were the most common contaminants observed. 

## Bias-related EDA code

The bias-related exploratory analysis examined missing values, ongoing violations, and possible imbalances across water system categories and counties.

```{python}

# Import final dataset
df = merged_df.copy()

# Missing value analysis
missing_values = df.isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
missing_percent = (df.isna().mean() * 100).sort_values(ascending=False)

print("Missing Values:")
print(missing_values)

print("\nMissing Percentage:")
print(missing_percent)

# visualize missing percentages
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
missing_percent.plot(kind='bar')
plt.title('Percentage of Missing Values by Column')
plt.ylabel('Percent Missing')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.show()


# Ongoing violations
# missing end_date values indicate unresolved or ongoing violations
df['ongoing_violation'] = df['end_date'].isna()

ongoing_counts = df['ongoing_violation'].value_counts()

print("\nOngoing Violations:")
print(ongoing_counts)

# visualize ongoing violations
plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
ongoing_counts.plot(kind='bar')
plt.title('Resolved vs Ongoing Violations')
plt.xticks([0,1], ['Resolved', 'Ongoing'], rotation=0)
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.show()


# County imbalance analysis
top_counties = df['county_served'].value_counts().head(15)

print("\nTop Counties by Violation Count:")
print(top_counties)

# visualize county imbalance
plt.figure(figsize=(12,5))
top_counties.plot(kind='bar')
plt.title('Top Counties by Violation Count')
plt.xlabel('County')
plt.ylabel('Violations')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.show()


# Water type imbalance
water_type_dist = df['water_type_code'].value_counts(dropna=False)

print("\nWater Type Distribution:")
print(water_type_dist)

# visualize water type imbalance
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
water_type_dist.plot(kind='bar')
plt.title('Distribution of Water Types')
plt.xlabel('Water Type')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.show()
```

## Bias-related EDA narrative

The bias-related exploratory analysis showed some possible limitations and imbalances in the dataset.

The missing value analysis showed that the water_type_code column had a large amount of missing data, with about 86% of records missing water source information. The county_served column also had missing values for about 24% of records. Missing location and water source information can make it harder to fully compare contamination trends across different areas and water system types.
The water system analysis showed that groundwater systems (GW) made up most of the reported water types, while surface water (SW) and purchased groundwater (GU) appeared much less often. This could mean groundwater systems are more common in the dataset, or that some systems do not report water source information consistently.
The county analysis also showed that some counties appeared much more often than others. Counties such as Lubbock and Midland had higher violation counts than many other counties. These differences could be related to population size, testing frequency, or reporting differences instead of contamination levels alone.
The dataset also mostly contains active facilities, while inactive facilities make up a much smaller part of the data. Active facilities are more likely to continue testing and reporting violations regularly.
Overall, the dataset is useful for identifying water quality trends and violations, but the missing data and reporting differences across facilities and counties should still be considered when looking at the results.

# Data Product & Guide

The final data product is a cleaned dataset containing drinking water violations, contaminant information, facility details, and county-level geographic information. The dataset was created by merging multiple EPA Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) datasets into one table.
The dataset is intended for environmental analysts, researchers, and public health officials interested in studying contamination trends and geographic patterns in drinking water quality.

## Final Dataset Variables

- pwsid: identifier for a public water system
- violation_id: identifier for a specific violation
- facility_id: identifier for a facility
- facility_name: name of the facility
- county_served: county served by the water system
- facility_status: whether the facility is active or inactive

- end_date: date the violation ended

# Extra Mile

This project required extra work to extract, clean, and merge multiple EPA datasets together. One challenge was standardizing contaminant codes because some datasets stored the values as decimals while others stored them as strings. Regular expression transformations were used to clean and standardize the contaminant codes before merging the datasets.
Additional work was also needed to reduce the size of the original datasets while keeping the important variables needed for analysis. Facility information, geographic data, contaminant reference codes, and violation records were filtered and merged into one final dataset.
The project also included extra exploratory analysis related to missing values, reporting differences, and possible imbalances across water system types and counties.
